summary:
Cabo Verde does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. Article 71 of the 1886 Penal Code prohibited unnatural acts; a 2004 amendment removed all provisions relating to consensual homosexual sex, making Cabo Verde the second country in Africa to decriminalise after South Africa. The age of consent stood at 16 at decriminalisation, the same as for consensual heterosexual acts; a source covering 2015 records it as 14.

No legal gender recognition framework is on record. Civil law blocked the change to a female legal name sought by Tchinda Andrade, the first publicly self-outed transgender woman in Cabo Verde, who came out in 1997 at age 19 and in a local newspaper in 1998; a 22 June 2016 interview records that refusal, and the sources contain no later statute or administrative procedure permitting a legal gender change. A visitor whose passport marker differs from presentation should expect no local precedent for documentary flexibility.

Workplace protection stops short of gender identity. Since 2008, articles 45(2) and 406(3) of the Labour Code have barred discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, with a fine set case by case, and article 406(3) applies the same penalty to unlawful dismissal on racial, ethnic, religious or sexual-orientation grounds. The sources record no equivalent statutory protection covering gender identity, and Cabo Verde is one of few African countries with any such workplace protection.

No same-sex union is recognised. On 11 July 2017 Prime Minister Ulisses Correia e Silva stated that legalising same-sex marriage was not on the government's agenda, following demands from the LGBT community for civil unions and marriage.

Trans-specific violence in this record is limited to one account. In the 2016 interview Tchinda Andrade reported verbal violence and two physical attacks in Cabo Verde, which the source does not date; no later trans-specific attack or killing is documented here.

The state's external posture is protective. Cabo Verde joined 65 other states on 18 December 2008 in a UN General Assembly statement affirming that human rights apply regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity and urging an end to criminal penalties on that basis; it signed UN documents in 2011 condemning violence and discrimination against LGBT people; it made anti-discrimination commitments in its 2024 Universal Periodic Review; and on 28 June 2025 it was the only African country to sign a 15-state foreign-ministers declaration rejecting criminalisation and stigmatisation, backing the eradication of transphobic harassment and socio-labour inclusion especially for trans persons, and calling for an end to conversion practices and to prosecution carrying imprisonment or death. Cabo Verde is one of two African members of the UN LGBTI Core Group.

Public-attitude data does not measure transgender acceptance. Polling records 82% of respondents in 2019–21 saying they would accept a 'homosexual' neighbour, and an Afrobarometer poll published in May 2020 found 80% of Cabo Verdeans would welcome or not be bothered by a homosexual neighbour, one of only four African countries polled with a majority in favour. Every tolerance finding in the sources is framed around gays, lesbians or homosexual neighbours, with none specific to transgender people. A 2010 US State Department Human Rights Report found that societal discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity continued to be a problem despite the legal provisions protecting homosexual conduct.
tangentialFactors:
LGBTIQ organisations register freely in Cabo Verde. The first public Pride was held in 2013, making Cabo Verde the second African country to hold one; the first Mindelo parade took place in June 2013 and the first Praia Pride three years later. The 2018 Pride Week in Praia combined a parade with campaigns by the Associação Gay de Cabo Verde, the Associação LGBTI de Praia and the Associação Arco Iris petitioning the National Assembly for same-sex marriage and an anti-discrimination law, with the state gender-equality institute ICIEG and UN Women engaged. Organisational life grew from no LGBT organisations recorded as active in 2010 to several by 2013.

Regional comparisons place Cabo Verde at the tolerant end of the continent. Afrobarometer's May 2020 dispatch identified Cabo Verde, Namibia and São Tomé and Príncipe as particularly tolerant countries, while finding that tolerance toward sexual minorities remains weak even among younger respondents across the region. The country has occasionally been described as the most tolerant in Africa with regard to LGBT people, though the same sources record continuing societal discrimination.

São Vicente is described as relaxed and known for being welcoming to the LGBT community, and Tchinda Andrade characterised Cabo Verde as markedly free for LGBT people compared with other African countries. These are LGB-framed reputational accounts; none of them addresses how transgender visitors are treated.
localsOnly:
Residents who work are covered by the Labour Code's sexual-orientation discrimination ban in articles 45(2) and 406(3), in force since 2008, with a fine determined case by case and the same penalty applied to discriminatory dismissal. Gender identity is not among the listed grounds.

Residents have no route to a recognised same-sex union or marriage, and no legal gender recognition procedure exists on record. Tchinda Andrade's blocked change to a female legal name, documented in 2016, is the only case of its kind in these sources.

Locals commonly refer to transgender people as 'tchindas'. LGBTIQ groups register without restriction and have organised Pride events since 2013, and the 2010 US State Department report, which found no lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender organisations active at that time, predates that growth.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the sources contain no statute, provision, penalty or procedure on gender markers in passports or identity cards, border or airport screening, segregated facilities, custody, or medical care for transgender people. Whether any administrative practice permits a marker change is likewise unsourced; only the 2016 refusal of a legal name change is documented.

Unresolved: whether the Labour Code's exclusion of gender identity from its discrimination grounds has since been amended is not addressed by any source here.

The age of consent figure of 14 is a 2015 snapshot and is not verified as the current value in these sources; the figure at decriminalisation in 2004 was 16.

No trans-specific violence count, killing tally or per-capita comparison appears in the inventory, so no trans violence rate can be stated. The only trans-specific harm documented is the undated verbal abuse and two physical attacks reported by Tchinda Andrade in her 2016 interview, and no later instance is documented.

All survey figures measure attitudes to homosexual neighbours or to gays and lesbians generally, not to transgender people, and none of the tolerance findings can be read as evidence about trans acceptance.
